Wish this could be a mixed review, because there is a lot to enjoy here. Game is fun, combining Balatro with Suika , and enough twists on the genre, and an cute aesthetic, which keep you going until you hit endless mode. Unfortunately at this point being able to basically go infinite with the right set-up means you could probably spend hours just dragging away at cards if you had the patience, which is not enjoyable. Having king dogs just turn in to ace dogs without any other effects I feel like is a design mistake, every other game in the Balatro style 'number go up' scoring formula has something in the mechanics which makes it harder to trap you in that endless cycle of play, but with the ever rising tide of dogs suddenly crashing back down as you combine your kings together, there's nothing here that really does that. Even worse, if you close in the middle of a run, then go back hoping to continue it, it doesn't work correctly. It keeps your progress on the score and with cash, but resets your deck, basically destroying that run! My fear is also that while there seems to be a lot of decks to unlock, that there won't be enough variety or challenge in the game to mean you keep playing until unlocking them all. Seems like a game to get burned out on after a few hours play. I might be wrong, as I'm not there yet, but while I do think this game is worth a play, I feel like there are still some big issues with it to get it anywhere close to that 'one more game' feeling that Balatro, and a couple of other games in the genre, manage to achieve. If they fix the issues with endless mode, and with continuing a run not losing your deck progress, then I'd probably still recommend it, but those issues are enough to tip it over to a no for me right now.

Dogpile is an inventive and charming indie title that blends deckbuilding, spatial puzzle design, and roguelike progression into a surprisingly cohesive whole. Developed collaboratively by Studio Folly, Toot Games, and Foot, and published by WINGS, the game revolves around a deceptively simple premise: playing cards that drop dogs into a vertical playfield, where matching breeds merge into larger, higher-value dogs. While the idea initially feels light and whimsical, it quickly reveals layers of strategic depth that reward foresight, adaptability, and a strong grasp of risk management. The result is a game that feels immediately approachable but steadily grows more demanding the longer a run continues. At the heart of Dogpile is its satisfying merge system, which turns spatial placement into a constant puzzle. Each dog card you play must be dropped into a crowded yard, and careless placement can rapidly lead to the pile reaching the top of the screen, triggering a tense countdown toward failure. Merging identical dogs not only clears space but also creates more valuable units that score better and unlock additional rewards, encouraging players to plan several moves ahead. This spatial awareness, combined with the randomness of card draws, creates an engaging push-and-pull between improvisation and long-term planning. Every decision feels consequential, as one poorly placed dog can unravel an otherwise promising run. The deckbuilding layer elevates Dogpile beyond a straightforward puzzle game. Cards can be upgraded, removed, or replaced between runs, allowing players to shape their deck toward specific strategies, whether that means aggressively chasing merges, focusing on space control, or building around certain dog types and bonuses. The roguelike structure ensures that no two runs play out the same, with modifiers and traits altering the rules in unexpected ways. Some traits offer powerful advantages that fundamentally change how the yard behaves, while others impose penalties that force players to rethink familiar tactics. These negative modifiers, often acquired after failure, add a sense of persistence and personality to each run, making setbacks feel like part of the learning process rather than simple punishment. Dogpile’s presentation plays a crucial role in maintaining its appeal during long sessions. The art style is colorful and expressive, with each dog brimming with personality that makes every merge feel rewarding on a visual level. Animations are snappy and readable, ensuring that even as the yard fills with dogs, the player can quickly assess the situation. The sound design complements the visuals with playful effects that reinforce the game’s lighthearted tone, preventing the tension of high-stakes moments from becoming stressful. This balance between charm and challenge gives Dogpile a cozy surface that masks a surprisingly demanding strategic core. Progression outside individual runs is thoughtfully designed to encourage experimentation. New cards, mechanics, and dogs are gradually unlocked, widening the pool of possibilities and ensuring that strategies continue to evolve. Rather than pushing players toward a single optimal build, Dogpile rewards curiosity, making it fun to test unconventional approaches even if they fail spectacularly. The game’s pacing is especially effective here, as runs are compact enough to invite repeated attempts, yet complex enough to make each one feel distinct and meaningful. There are minor rough edges, particularly in how some mechanics are explained, as new players may need several runs before fully understanding how certain modifiers interact. However, this learning curve feels consistent with the game’s roguelike philosophy, and the satisfaction of mastering its systems far outweighs any initial confusion. Overall, Dogpile stands out as a clever fusion of genres, delivering an experience that is both endearingly playful and mechanically rich. It is a game that draws players in with its adorable premise and keeps them engaged through smart design, strategic depth, and a constant sense of discovery, making it a memorable addition to the indie deckbuilding and puzzle space. Rating: 8/10

A really good and fun mashup of Suika game and roguelike, the latter of which is one of my favorite subgenres. There's pretty decent build variety with the different traits and tags. Although in terms of traits friendly is easily the strongest one, unlike the pack trait which I found quite weak and barely used throughout my 25 hours of completing everything, even when using the pack centered deck I veered towards using a different trait for my build. Also, this could just be a skill issue on my part, but I felt that the threshold for losing was a little unforgiving sometimes. If even a pixel of one of your dogs was poking out the top the timer would appear and if you couldn't move it, merge it, or get rid of it in some way you would lose. Overall, I enjoyed my time with this game and had a blast completing all the decks (except pedigree, ♥♥♥♥ pedigree, though thankfully it wasn't required for the achievement). If any future content updates are in the works, I would gladly hop back in.

Yo, shoutout to dogs, but they've gotta have some of the worst representation in gaming. Maybe I'm just more of a cat person, but I feel like half the time you see a game with or about dogs, it's that "pet teh heckin' pupper" brand of humor... gross... Thankfully "Dogpile" steers clear from this pitfall and delivers a game that is, dare I say, pretty funny! Not necessarily "haha funny," but I had a good chuckle. Unfortunately, that's about where my praise ends—"good dog jokes." Past that, I found this game to be largely underwhelming; seeing all it had to offer in just over two hours and, after that, finding the game just didn't take its core mechanics seriously enough to make dedicating the time to 𝗴𝗶𝘁 𝗴𝘂𝗱 even remotely interesting for me. On the surface, Dogpile is advertised as a roguelike/deck-builder/merge game hybrid—what a mouthful! While I've adamantly avoided this whole 'deck builder psy-op,' the tacked-on mechanics of a merge game drew me in like a pie resting on a windowsill; merge games like 2048, Triple Town, and Cow Evolution used to be my sh!t, I envisioned a game with the satisfying puzzle-solving of a merge game, formatted to be as strategic and replayable as a roguelike... but this excitement only left me frustrated and blue-balled. When this game says it's a roguelike, what it's really trying to say is that it's just random, and that clashes with the puzzle-solving aspect in a way that is just too chaotic for me. Like, imagine you were trying to solve a jig-saw puzzle, right? Except your only way to solve the puzzle was by going absolute ape-sh!t and smashing the table around until you happened to knock the pieces together. Sound like fun? Now imagine you finally start getting some matches, so I tell you, "Okay, for this next turn you can either select a puzzle piece by hand... or you can just keep smashing the table, even harder!" Hopefully, that makes sense because that's exactly what playing this game feels like. I had the most fun when I had perks that gave me more control over what was happening, which was entirely down to RNG that was not in my favor. It's fine for a game to be zany, and at times it's even enjoyable here, but this game feels like it's screaming for your dedicated improvement only to huck a garbage can at you when you try to better understand it. Dogpile is cute and quirky but overall feels like missed potential. Probably super comfy on the Steam Deck, though; if the trailer looks appealing to you and you don't mind what I've just described, then I can absolutely recommend the game when it's on sale.

A while back I read a negative review of this game that called it “as repetitive as tetris” and I don't think anyone could give it a better compliment. I have to admit I had my reservations going into this game, I feared this was a case of style over substance, and make no mistake, the presentation of this game is without a doubt its strongest quality, but I find the gameplay quite compelling as well. after the success of Balatro it seems like every other indie release is a remix of an innocuous classic game with rogue-like additions, this particular archetype of game has its benefits and challenges; the foundation of your game is strong as is, which means a big part of the process of conceptualization is basically done, the challenge is to make an experience that is fresh and fun without overdoing it and overpowering the fun qualities of the thing you’re remixing. The question, then, is whether Dogpile is successful in this ambition; if you’ve played any other rogue-like you will be in part familiar with the systems within the game, you have your individual modifiers that affect a single card, your multiple modifiers, you have the classics like “this card now gives you extra X of the specific currency” or “playing this card draws more cards” as well as some that could only work in a suika type game, all of them lovingly designed to be consistent to the theme, and speaking of which: You can buy dog tags at the dog store, you can upgrade or enchant you cards are the dog wash, when you don't meet your quota of bones (put a pin in these) you get disciplined, but again, this game is more than just well groomed, it can be quite difficult at times and to win you need to be aware of the board as well as your modifiers, some that appear to be exclusively negative can, just with buying a single tag, turn into run savers. Let’s go back to the bones, in this game you manage two currencies, you have your money and bones, the former is rather self explanatory, you get money by merging dogs and use that money to buy either tags or other cards, bones however, get a bit tricky; you need to meet a bones quota every so often, you get bones in the same way you get money, but if you don't get enough bones you are penalized, the run doesn't end but you need to pick one of two debuffs, the cool thing about being disciplined is that the possible debuffs are all no different from your negative modifiers, and therefore they can be affected by tags, so if you're clever and your built is right, failing a bones quota can literally win you the game. So, to answer the question, I think Dogpile does succeed in its ambition and is quite a fun game. If you want my recommendation I say you unlock the challenges as soon as possible, that's where i think the game truly shines.

What DOES interest me is: -dogs -whimsy -cute art There’s obviously some chaos with the randomness of some runs, and sure, I fail a lot- But, the game has a lot of personality and love poured into it. It makes me giggle and smile and laugh, and yes occasionally shout in dismay. If you need more engagement during the game loop, listen to music, talk to friends in a call, listen to a podcast. The world is your oyster, but the cute dogs have you at an advantage. I was really happy they added more content, and it’s a game I’ll be going back to for a while, especially when I need to smile.

Dogpile is [i][b]dumb[/b][/i]. It's silly, stupid and simple fun. You like dogs? You like silly game concepts? Or maybe you're looking for a game you don't have to think too hard to play, something you can launch to play an idle 15 minute round of total nonsense to enjoy. Dogpile fills that spot decently. It's okay. However, I cannot [i]strongly[/i] reccomend Dogpile. I won't lie, there's problems with the game that arise very quickly the moment you focus on it too hard or try to take it too seriously. The core gameplay is fine, good even, but a lot of design choices piled [i](ha)[/i] on top of that core gameplay is... [b]very[/b] poorly thought out. Challenge decks and the process of unlocking new content is by far among the worst offenders. In order for me to enjoy this game, I had to quickly disengage with the gimmicks and stop caring about deeper mechanics simply because it would otherwise turn it into a chore, which isn't a great look for Dogpile. But I had fun with it- and any game that can unironically make me utter phrases like "The Air Bud Infinite" and have me giggling at the absurdity of it all is definitely worth at some consideration, at least when it's at a low asking price.

Dogpile is a well made Suika game with a cute art style, the gameplay is fun and the perks do a solid job at changing how you play a run. Some runs you can get wild infinites, but its not every time. I do wish the endless mode wasn't as punishing, sometimes it gives you modifiers that just kill your run. I personally feel I also tend to lean into certain traits a lot more than others. Things like Dig and Zoomy are really good, and that in itself isn't a problem but it does feel to me that some other traits have trouble keeping up. I also do appreciate the fact that one of the decks is just straight Suika. No Perks no modifiers. Lets you just play without the wacky stuff if you want. Didn't need to be added but I think its a great addition. Overall I would recommend it if you like Suika games, Its quick relaxing fun that you don't have to worry to much about, and as a bonus it has simple enough achievements if you like going for 100% too.
